subject: bigRig
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: chrome big-rig truck.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I'm brainstorming an unexpected art style for this chrome big-rig truck build, considering options like dieselpunk pop-art with Ben-Day halftone dots that I could realistically render with paint and SVG.

Settling on Art Deco Streamline Moderne — black lacquer, jade, and gold sunburst inlays with chevrons, ziggurat steps, and fan motifs against polished chrome. Now I need to write careful, robust code without being able to test it, aiming for roughly 250 parts across 600-800 lines using simple part-building APIs.

Since this is a static truck model, I don't strictly need joints, but I'll add a minimal rig anyway: a root "chassis" joint plus wheel joints for rotation, keeping it simple and skipping unnecessary hinges like doors.

I'm picturing a full tractor-trailer rig for extra visual appeal, a chrome Art Deco tanker trailer paired with the tractor, with realistic scale around 20 meters total length and a triangle budget comfortably under 60k.

I'm now setting up coordinate constants: wheel radius and tire width, tractor positioned toward the front with the trailer extending behind, and working out track width and dual-wheel spacing so the tires sit properly under the body.

Then I'm sketching the frame rails and starting the tractor layout, placing the front axle and beginning the hood shape for a conventional-style chrome cab.

Now I'm detailing the grill, fenders, and cab/sleeper proportions, giving the sleeper a stepped Deco roofline and dark teal glass with gold sunburst reflections, then adding tall chrome exhaust stacks behind the cab.

I'm placing the stacks near the cab's rear corners beside the narrowed sleeper, adjusting positions to avoid exceeding the trailer width, and planning the tandem drive axles plus fifth wheel plate connection point before moving on to the trailer's kingpin layout.

For the tanker itself, I'm designing a lathed tube along the z-axis with domed caps at each end, defining a rounded profile from axis to rim and back to create a smooth, chrome-like cylindrical tank with enough segments for a polished rather than faceted look.

Now I need the taillights, landing gear, and trailer sub-chassis with axles near the rear, plus wheels sized with radius 0.52. For the chrome finish, I'm designing a custom paint function based on surface normal direction that fakes a sky-to-ground reflection—dark ground tones below the horizon, a sharp bright band at the horizon line, and a blue-white (or gold sunrise) sky above.

I'm leaning toward an Art Deco sunset palette: deep indigo ground, hot gold horizon band, and a sky gradient from cream to teal to deep blue at the top, plus sunburst ray stripes based on angle and some fine noise-based streaks for realism, including a window-reflection stripe along the tank body at a specific normal angle.

For paint resolution, I'm estimating texel density across the truck's surface area to pick an atlas size—2048px should get roughly 1cm texels, which is fine detail-wise, so I'll reserve painted textures for the tank, hood, and tractor while keeping other parts flat-colored to save atlas space. I'm also noting that the high-frequency sunburst lines will need finer texture detail than the base paint density allows.

Now I'm sketching out the decal textures needed: a Deco sunburst emblem for grille and doors, a teal windshield gradient with gold pinstripe, a door-side logo reading "GOLDEN ARROW FREIGHT" with fan rays, concentric sunburst headlight lenses, and ring-patterned tire sidewalls with hub cap star designs.

I'm also planning the trim details — chevron pinstripe bands along the cab sides, tail light lenses, a "RIG-1937" license plate, and keeping the interior simple with dark glass instead of visible dash details. For the mud flap, I'm considering a classic chrome Deco silhouette figure, though I want to keep the pose simplified so it doesn't look awkward.

For applying decals onto curved surfaces, I'm deciding to use flat PlaneGeometry panels textured with the designs instead, since they're more robust than true curved decals. I'm writing a helper function for placing these textured plates with correct orientation, direction, and "up" axis so the artwork reads correctly when viewed from either side of the truck.

Working through the vector math confirms the left-side plate orientation is correct — text will read front-to-rear as expected from the viewer's perspective. Now I'm planning to keep the color palette tidy, limiting it to at most 64 flat colors.

I'm defining the palette: lacquer black, jade and jade-dark for fenders, gold for trims, cream, burgundy, rubber black, glass texture, and accent reds/ambers/steel for lamps and hardware. The overall styling leans into Art Deco Streamline Moderne — chrome tank with horizontal speed-line grooves and Deco fin ornaments to reinforce the motif.

For the hood ornament I'm considering a stylized chrome flying figure or swept-back fan-ribbed arrow shape as a signature element, then moving into the actual geometry plan — setting up a builder with a named rig and paint texture size, defining joint hierarchy starting with a chassis root, and establishing a helper to place body parts onto that chassis bone by default, with a separate trailer joint parented at the kingpin for articulation and wheel joints parented to the chassis for front/rear positioning.

I'm working out joint orientation conventions — using a direction vector so cylindrical tire geometry aligns its axis correctly when placed — and writing a placement helper function to simplify attaching parts to the chassis bone with position and extra options, keeping types loose to avoid strictness issues. Now I'm defining the wheel construction logic, starting with the tire's cylinder dimensions and radial segments.

For the tire shape itself, I'm considering a lathe profile instead of a plain cylinder so I can round the shoulders and add subtle tread grooves, sketching out the outline points that trace the rubber's cross-section from one sidewall to the other.

Adding a gold whitewall pinstripe ring to the tires, reorienting the torus to face along the wheel axis instead of its default plane.

Each wheel assembly needs a tire, chrome hub cylinder, nut ring, and hub detail texture—roughly five parts per wheel. With 18 wheel positions total across the front axle, dual rear axles, and trailer, I'm estimating part budget to keep the scene manageable.

Dual-wheel setups need an inner tire plus an outer tire with its own hub, offset outward along the axle. I'm also considering adding streamlined fender spats over the trailer's tandem axles using arched half-cylinders to match that moderne aesthetic.

Checking the thickness needed to span the dual wheel width, I settle on a fender thickness of 0.75 centered at x=0.95 to cover the 0.6 to 1.3 range properly, keeping it as a thin arch shell.

Now for the tandem axles, I'm designing a longer skirt spat that covers both axles as one continuous streamlined shape rather than two separate arches—outlining a stadium-shaped hollow polygon that forms the covering fender.

Still working out fender dimensions...

Raising the tank center to 2.2 keeps it under the legal height limit with clearance to the tractor roof, giving room for a saddle-block cradle between the frame rails and tank bottom. I'll match the drive-axle fenders on the tractor to the same arch style as the trailer, just differentiated by color and trim.

Now I'm working out the tractor's longitudinal layout: steer axle around z=5.6, drive tandem near z=-0.1 and -1.4, fifth wheel just ahead of the tandem center at roughly z=-0.55, and the trailer kingpin/front dome starting near z=-0.7 to -1.0. With a 12.5m trailer length, it ends near z=-13.5, placing the tandem axles around z=-11.4 and -12.7, and the front bumper extending to about z=7.5.

I'm defining the cab's side-profile silhouette with a sloped windshield, then extruding it along the x-axis to build the full 3D shape, with the extrusion direction oriented so the outline runs rearward.

Continuing the roof line toward the sleeper top, then curving down the rounded rear with a streamline-moderne taper into the back corner — I need to watch for self-intersection risk where smoothing meets short edges, so I'll keep tighter smoothing values near those sharp transitions.

I'm splitting the extrude into two separate profiles with different widths: a thicker cab section and a thinner sleeper section with a tiered ziggurat-style roof topper, then planning a height-based two-tone paint scheme with jade below, a gold accent band, and black above.

I'm designing a custom lacquer paint function that darkens surfaces based on normal direction and adds a subtle glossy highlight streak, plus a two-tone variant for the cab that switches color by y-position so both parts share consistent shading logic.

Now I'm positioning the side window decals symmetrically on the cab and sleeper, then working out the windshield's tilted plane geometry by computing tangent and normal vectors from the slope between its bottom and top edge points.

For the window geometry, I'm calculating the quadrilateral bounds for the slanted cab window, factoring the top slope, and planning a chamfered glass texture with stepped Deco corners cut away to reveal the body beneath. For the door, I'm sketching gold pinstripe trim, a chrome handle, an emblem, and a transparent SVG texture with Deco-style outline corners.

Now I'm sizing the door plane and figuring viewBox-to-stroke scaling so pinstripes render crisply at roughly 3px, then thinking through how mirrored cab sides should read — since real trucks display text left-to-right from the viewer's perspective, the mural orientation needs to flip appropriately between the left and right sides so the front of the truck reads consistently on each side.

For the hood, I'm planning to use a lofted shape through several stations to get a tapered, rounded Deco-style profile rather than a simple extrusion, sketching out approximate station positions and widths to build that signature streamlined hood shape.

For the grille, I'm thinking of vertical chrome/gold slats arranged in a fan pattern, framed by an arched Deco surround with stepped edges, topped with a sunburst emblem plane.

The grill frame sits around z 6.97-7.07 with slats layered at 7.06, so the rounded loft cap shouldn't poke through noticeably. Now I'm placing a Deco "flying arrow" hood ornament near the front-top of the hood, roughly centered at the hood's midline height around z 6.7-6.95.

Then I'm sketching the chrome wraparound bumper as a swept box section following a polyline path that curves out and back at the front corners.

Still working out bumper geometry...

For the headlights, I'm thinking streamline moderne bullet-shaped pods mounted on the fenders, chrome-finished with lens glow, positioned near the front corners, with jade swooping fenders arcing over the wheels.

Still placing components...

Still writing stack lathe profile...

Checking stack placement against the sleeper width—the stack sits just slightly beyond the cab's edge, so I'll widen the cab a touch and add a bracket box connecting the muffler/stack assembly to the sleeper wall to keep things tidy.

Now I'm working out the mirrors: a chrome strut rod running from the cab corner out to a mirror housing box, with a reflective glass plane facing rearward toward the back of the truck.

For headlights, I'm placing bullet-shaped lamp pods on chrome stalks mounted atop the front fenders, positioning them near the hood sides with the lens facing forward and figuring out the lathe profile for that classic Deco bullet shape.

Finishing the lens pod profile ending flat at the front, and planning a gold visor ring around it. I'm also thinking about adding glow effects for headlamps using an emissive clone technique, and considering amber marker lights along the cab roof.

For Deco styling on the sleeper roof, I'm stacking three decreasing box tiers like a ziggurat in jade and gold, plus adding tapering chrome speed-fin streaks along the body side using a gradient texture to echo the streamline look.

Now I'm placing a sunburst star emblem on the sleeper side and planning the fifth wheel plate, chassis frame rails, crossmembers, and axles beneath the cab in black to form the undercarriage structure.

Adding wheel axles, differential housing, leaf spring stacks, and basic air tank/driveshaft details, then setting up the trailer as its own bone with black frame rails and chrome landing gear legs positioned toward the rear.

For the tandem axle wheels at the trailer's rear, and the tank body itself, I'm defining a lathe profile along the trailer axis to shape the rounded tank ends and straight midsection.

I want to use enough segments for smooth chrome shading on the tank, and I'm thinking about adding a subtle horizon reflection strip based on surface normal to sell the chrome look.

Writing chrome paint function...

Writing skyline silhouette logic...

I realize using azimuth alone gives constant bands along the tank's length since the axis runs along z, so I'm mixing in position along the tank with the azimuth angle to get variation, like a passing skyline reflection, then adding subtle noise for imperfection in brightness.

I'm sticking with a single chrome variant for consistency across small parts, then defining a reusable lacquer paint function that blends a dark and light tone based on surface normal, adds a bright highlight streak near the top, and includes a window-shine stripe effect.

For the cab I'm layering a vertical two-tone paint scheme, jade lower, black roof, with a gold dividing line, cutting out the window regions so the color bands stay visible around them, and mirroring the beltline detail. Then I'm moving on to placing gold ring bands around the tank.

Still working out tank ring placement...

Actually a flat plane won't hug the curved tank surface properly, so I should use a decal projection instead -- wrapping the logo texture directly onto the tank's lathe geometry with a defined position, direction, and size so it conforms to the curve rather than floating off the surface.

For orientation, I'm reasoning through how "dir" and "up" determine which way the decal faces and reads: for the left side (dir toward +X), a viewer standing at +X sees the text running toward the rear; for the right side (dir toward -X), the "right" direction flips so text reads front-to-rear instead, which seems consistent with how decals auto-orient from dir/up. I'm also sanity-checking the default segment count against the decal's 5-meter length to make sure the mesh resolution is reasonable.

For the decal target, I confirm that a Part itself can serve as the surface argument since "surface" accepts anything with that interface.

Now I'm sketching the logo SVG itself: a wide 500x150 viewBox with an Art Deco half-sunburst motif on the left in gold and black, bold Deco-style lettering spelling "GOLDEN ARROW" with wide letter-spacing (falling back to generic sans-serif since fancy fonts won't rasterize), black fill with a gold stroke to stand out against the chrome tank, plus speed lines and an arrow accent, with a smaller "FREIGHT & LIQUID LINES" subtitle beneath. Since the texture is transparent outside the drawn shapes, only the front-facing decal shapes will actually show once applied.

For the tank's top, I'm planning a long, narrow catwalk platform with Deco-style ribbing details.

Positioning the catwalk platform along the tank's curved top, I'm adding three chrome manway hatches (domed lathe shapes) spaced along the length, each with a gold trim ring, hinge lugs, and a bolt ring, built from a simple rotated profile. For safety rails, I'm placing support posts every couple meters along both sides of the catwalk with top rails running between them, keeping the overall height comfortably under the legal trailer height limit and below the tractor roofline. At the rear, I'm adding a chrome ICC bumper bar along with Deco-style taillights made of stacked vertical red lens pods mounted near the back corners.

Working out exact placement, I'm mounting the taillight pods on brackets extending from the rear frame so they clear the tapering rear dome of the tank -- checking the radius math confirms the pods sit outside the tank's curved surface at that point. I'm also considering a rear ladder near the tank's rear dome slope but may skip it if the curvature makes mounting awkward.

I'm positioning mud flaps as single-sided planes with a chrome-silhouette texture behind each rear tandem wheel set, checking the wheel edge positions and tank end to make sure the flaps hang just clear of the trailer's rear axle without clipping.

I'm doing the same for the tractor's drive tandem, checking clearances against the trailer front and frame rails, and then planning to add coiled air brake hoses between the tractor and trailer using a sweep geometry.

Writing helix sweep code...

Thinking about which bone to parent this to — probably the chassis bone since it spans cab to trailer. Now checking the fifth wheel positioning relative to the tank bottom to make sure they don't clip.

Checking the tank bottom clearance against the rail top near z=-1.8, then adding small cradle ring support boxes along the trailer at a few z positions to fill the gap, before moving to the kingpin coupling plate region near z=-0.9.

I'm positioning amber marker lights along the trailer rails, then working out aero skirt panels beneath the tank sides — calculating tank radius at x=1.1 to size a floating skirt box between the axles, mounted via struts to the frame.

Now I'm adding Deco ornamental details: jade lacquer skirts with gold pinstripe accents, and gold speed-fin extrusions on the tractor's front fender tops, defining a swept fin outline profile for the shape.

I'm figuring out the joint hierarchy for the wheels, setting up an axle joint helper that positions and orients each wheel relative to the chassis root, then naming the various drive and trailer wheel bones (front, dual drive axles, dual trailer axles, left/right pairs).

I'm making sure the chassis joint comes first as the root, then the trailer joint parented to it, then wheels using mirrored left/right placement loops. I'm also checking the tire contact point so the flattened bottom vertices of the lathed cylinder sit essentially at y=0, nudging the wheel center down slightly to compensate for the polygon approximation.

Now I'm defining the hub plate geometry and positioning it at the wheel center to bridge the tire's hollow inner radius.

Adding hub cap detail...

Still writing tire profile logic...

I'm noting that the lathe's s[1] parameter wraps at the 360° seam, which could cause minor interpolation artifacts across seam triangles, but it's a small enough issue to ignore. Now I'm sketching out the list of texture assets I'll need, starting with a sunburst grille emblem medallion and a windshield texture with diagonal glints and a pinstripe edge.

Rounding out the texture list: side windows with chamfered corners, door trim, a tank logo, a headlamp lens with concentric rings and sunburst, a tail lens with chevrons, a deco star hub fan, a flap silhouette, speed lines, a mirror glass variant, and a license plate — eleven textures total. Now I'm defining the SVG viewBox dimensions for each and starting to write the gradient definition for the glass texture.

Still writing SVG code...

I realize the right side window needs mirroring since front/rear sides flip depending on viewer orientation, so I'll create a flipped version of the side window texture using a transform rather than redrawing it, keeping the door and sunburst trim symmetric so no flip is needed there.

Writing door outline paths...

Working out exact coordinates for the door and window placement within the cab, computing their centers and dimensions relative to the cab's z-range so the window sits nested inside the door with consistent margins.

I'm placing a sunburst medallion window on the sleeper side with decorative speed-line decals, and checking that the cab's width transition from the hood smoothly widens at the back station.

Checking the hood-to-cab cowl junction, the windshield bottom aligns with the hood top height, and estimating total part count across wheels, chassis, cab, tank, and trailer comes to roughly 250 pieces. Now I'm setting up the imports and beginning the build script...

Writing color palette constants...

Still writing skyline silhouette logic...

Working out the color typing...

The skyline boundary at 0.58 looks fine, with reflection normals handling the gold horizon and dark ground correctly where decals sit. Now I'm writing a lacquer paint function that blends dark and light colors based on surface normal, adds a specular highlight near the top, then layers subtle noise variation into the brightness.

Writing CAB paint layers...

Setting up wheel joints and the axle table...

Still defining lathe profile points...

Now I'm building the hubcap out of a chromed cylinder cap with a circular hub face textured with the logo, cropped by the circle geometry.

Good, that checks out since the smaller circle sits within the tire solid and stays hidden behind it. Now I'm working out dual wheel spacing — inner and outer tire centers with gaps between them, versus the single front tire width — and planning a gold pinstripe torus ring on the tire sidewall, positioned in the flat region between the hub hole and outer edge with a small tube radius.

Now I'm adding the axle, differential housing, and leaf spring details, deciding to skip lug nuts and keep springs only on the drive axles. I'm also blocking out the chassis rails as long boxes spanning front to back and starting on the crossmembers.

Continuing with the front axle cylinder, skipping the hidden engine/radiator, and adding a driveshaft segment. I'm placing the fifth wheel as a flat chrome-steel cylinder with a notch, positioned where the chassis rails end, plus a skid plate under the trailer's front.

I'm adding an upper coupler box on the trailer, fuel tanks and battery box, and skipping the chrome air tanks behind the steps. For the running boards, I'm sizing and positioning them relative to the cab's half-width so they stay within a reasonable legal width.

Adding gold rib details to the step treads and planning chrome louver fins as Deco speed-grills on the hood sides.

Since the hood's cross-section shape is uncertain, I realize I should use a surface raycasting approach instead of guessing coordinates -- casting a ray from outside the hood to find the actual surface hit point, then sticking the louver geometry there. This is more robust against buried or floating geometry from the loft shape.

For the louver sticks themselves, I'm working out orientation: the box geometry's height dimension should align with the local normal, with flow set along the z-axis so the louvers run lengthwise along the hood's surface direction, embedding partially into the surface for a seamless look.

I'm shifting to safer surface-hit approaches for details like louvers and the hood ornament—casting rays downward onto the hood to find placement points, then using those hit coordinates to position pedestals and extruded wing shapes. Now I'm planning chrome air horns mounted on the cab roof, likely as paired cone or lathe shapes.

Still writing horn lathe profile...

Now I'm working out the windshield geometry—positioning the slanted plane between the hood slope and roof edge, computing its center and normal vector, and sizing it narrower than the cab width to leave frame margins on each side.

I'm deciding to skip decorative elements on the lower cab front and sleeper back since they're mostly hidden behind the hood anyway, then moving on to placing chrome door handle boxes along the door's rear edge near z=3.0.

I'll add a sunburst emblem circle to the door's lower panel, then work out the sleeper's side geometry — keeping its width slightly narrower than the cab so the transition reads cleanly — and start defining its extrusion profile points for the roofline taper.

Still writing profile points...

There's a slight roofline step between cab and sleeper, which is acceptable. I'm sizing the bevel on the extrudes to stay within half the wall thickness, and building the sleeper's tiered crown decoration with stacked boxes shrinking in size toward the top, alternating jade and gold, plus a fin rib and possibly a gold sunburst detail on the front face.

I'm placing oval chrome-ringed porthole windows on both sides of the sleeper with a teal glass and sunburst texture, and adding speed-line graphics lower on the emblem area. Estimating around 700 lines of code total, I'm moving forward with careful SVG texture definitions for things like the sunburst medallion emblem.

Writing SVG code...

Designing the tail shape and flap mudflap graphics...

Now I'm designing the mirror, plate, and logo elements: a gradient sky mirror, a cream plate with "GOLDEN ST 1938" text, and a sunburst logo with layered gold-and-black "GOLDEN ARROW" text for a chrome-like outlined effect.

Still writing logo SVG...

I'm placing the logo centered around z=-6.6, then adding the front and rear dome tank sections with catwalks, hatches, and a small rear valve cabinet for detail. I'll finish the tank with chrome paint and gold decorative ring bands.

Writing ring geometry code...

Designing the tail light pods as chrome rectangular boxes with glowing lens planes facing rearward, plus mounting brackets connecting them to the rail.

Now I'm positioning amber side marker lights along the skirt panel's outer face at regular intervals along the trailer length, working out the correct offsets based on skirt thickness and height.

I'm also considering adding a speed-stripe texture to the skirt panels, reusing the gold/cream taper design but needing to flip it depending on the side so the streaks always trail toward the rear visually—planning a flip parameter for each texture generator function.

Skipping hood and dome details for now, I'm focusing on the fender arches: thinking about painting the extruded rim gold while keeping the flat faces jade, distinguishing them by checking the surface normal direction.

So actually it's the walls (big curved surface) that get jade and the thin edge faces that get gold—opposite of what I first assumed. For the fender paint function I'm checking if the normal's x-component exceeds a threshold to decide gold versus jade, while trailer fenders just get solid chrome. Now I'm sketching the arch outline helper that builds the extrusion coordinates.

Writing arch extrusion code...

I'm defining the OutlinePoint type and checking the superellipse sample count gives a good arch shape. Now I'm sizing the tandem fender for the tractor's drive axles, checking clearances against the sleeper floor and fuel tank placement to make sure nothing overlaps.

Checking that the drive fenders don't collide with the trailer tank's position confirms things clear fine. I'm now sizing the front fender arch and adding a pylon for the headlight at its top, then sketching a gold speed fin accessory to extrude onto the front fenders.

Writing fin outline coordinates...

After that I'll move on to the cab glass and a dark recessed grille block for the radiator shell.

Still shaping the grille slats...

Still working out ziggurat geometry...

Now I'm thinking about where to place the emblem medallion relative to the grille slats, since the slats' top tier might overlap with a natural spot for it. I'll try shortening the slat recess height so there's clear space on the gold plate's upper tier for the emblem circle.

Centering the medallion between the slat top and crest top gives a diameter around 0.36, which fits within the tier width there. I'll stop fine-tuning the numbers and move to defining the hood shape itself, lofting it through three tapering stations from the base up toward the grille.

I'm confirming the loft works with three stations, and that the fenders' width stays clear of the hood's maximum half-width so nothing overlaps. Then I'm casting rays against the hood surface to find mounting points for details, and setting up a loop to place side louvers by raycasting against the skin at several heights and sizes.

Now I'm sketching the hood ornament: raycasting down from above to find the mounting point, then building a small pedestal via a lathe profile and a flying-arrow shape via extrusion, choosing chrome and gold materials for the louvers and trim.

Still working out the geometry...

Still defining wing geometry...

For the air-line, I'm writing a helper that generates a helical path of points using cosine/sine offsets stepping along an axis, then sweeps a thin tube along that catmull-rom curve with a small radius and polygon sides to form coiled tubing on the chassis.

I'm skipping soot/paint details on the exhaust stacks for now. I'm defining shorthand helper functions for placing parts on the trailer versus chassis bones, and a plate helper that builds a textured plane geometry oriented with a direction and optional up vector, handling the case where up is undefined via conditional spreading.

I'm adding a disc helper for circular textured plates and a glow wrapper, but noting glow only works on flat-colored or textured materials, not painted ones -- windows with dark glass should stay non-glowing while white-textured parts are fine. I'm also being careful to avoid unused imports or parameters since the TypeScript setup seems strict about that, so I'll make sure the rng import and any paint callback parameters are actually used.

Now I'm setting up imports from the builder library along with THREE and the glow kit, defining color constants for the art deco palette (blacks, jades, golds, creams, chrome tones), and sketching helper functions and paint colors for sky gradients, horizon bands, and chrome highlights.

Writing color constants...

Building the emblem circle with gold rays and layered rings...

Now sketching the hub icon with a chrome radial gradient, gold ring and spokes, plus smaller lens and tail shapes for the remaining parts of the set.

Still writing SVG assets... then moving to the main builder code setting up the chassis joint for the golden arrow rig.

Setting dual wheel offsets and defining a tread paint function that darkens sidewalls and alternates tread block colors by position.

Now I'm laying out axle shaft geometry connecting the two sides at proper length and positioning, then adding a chrome differential sphere at the axle center for drive/tandem axles.

I'm switching to steel for the shaft parts, attaching them statically to the axle bone, and planning box-shaped springs for the front, drive, and tandem axles. Then I'm working out the cab geometry, extruding a side-profile outline along the correct thickness direction using cross products to determine the local axis orientation.

Now I'm adjusting the bevel value down slightly to avoid issues with sharp or concave corners, and designing a roof visor as a tilted box positioned at the cab's front edge, matching the slope and corner coordinates of the roofline.

I'm placing roof marker lights above the visor, then double-checking the overall cab silhouette height and total vehicle length to keep everything proportionate.

Now I'm building out the cab side details for both left and right: door trim, windows, handles, emblem discs, step boards with ribs, mirrors, exhaust stacks and mufflers with brackets, and sleeper side elements.

I'm also checking that the door window geometry aligns properly with the cab's z-depth, verifying the side window texture orientation flips correctly between left and right, and confirming the plate's up-vector and quaternion alignment work for side-mounted panels. Now I'm moving on to the fuel tank, front fenders with fins, headlamps on pylons, and drive fenders with flaps.

For the headlamp pods, I'm positioning lathe-generated shapes with supporting pylon rods connecting to the chassis, adding glowing lens discs and gold visor rings, while checking the pod placement clears the hood and sits above the fender bounds. I'm finishing up the front bumper details and starting on the tow hitch.

Now I'm planning landing gear legs as retracted stubby struts with foot pads near the rear underside, and figuring out the hatch details—dome, bolt ring, and lug—to keep each one modest at three components per hatch across three hatches.

For the catwalk, I'm positioning posts along the tank's length with connecting top rails, then placing the deck plank itself, but I'm noticing the post positions need adjusting since the tank's curved surface rises above where I'd planned the deck height.

I'll make the deck dark steel colored instead of adding stripes, and have the hatch domes sit directly on top of the deck surface so they clear the curve properly. Now I'm moving on to writing the code that stacks up the tank's ring segments for the lathe outline.

Checking the lathe profile rule, the points need to trace out from the axis around the shape and loop back to it, which my sequence does correctly since it starts and ends at x=0. I'm setting up the tank as a lathe shape attached to the trailer bone, oriented along the z-axis, chrome colored, with 24 segments for smoothness.

Now I'm placing a logo decal on the tank's side, considering mirroring for the opposite flank and whether decals inherit the tank's rigid attachment to the trailer. I'm also thinking about adding a stylized dorsal fin ornament along the top of the tank for a deco streamline look.

For the rear of the tank, I'm figuring out where a small emblem medallion should sit on the rounded dome end, checking the radius and z-offset of the dome's curve so the disc sits flush against the tapered tip rather than floating above it.

This positioning math is getting too fiddly—better to just decal the disc directly onto the tank surface instead of hand-calculating offsets.

Now I'm structuring the final module: chassis beams, then working through the full part list systematically.

Still positioning the fuel tank and checking clearances, then adding gold strap rings to hold it in place.

Still placing steps and ribs...

I'm working out where the coil hose should terminate so it visually touches the tank dome surface, adjusting the z-coordinate until the radius matches, and adding small cylinder fittings at the hose ends. For the colors, I'll use red for the left helix and a yellow/amber tone for the right one.

Next I'm adding a mounting plate box behind the sleeper, then checking the fifth wheel's apron plate position against the tank's radius profile to make sure they don't visually collide—a small overlap near z=-1.3 seems acceptable. Still need to place landing gear, working everything out relative to the trailer's coordinate frame.

Now I'm laying out the trailer frame itself: side rails running the length, with wheel cradles spaced at several z positions that sit just below the tank with a slight tolerable overlap, plus horizontal struts connecting the rails to the skirt. I'm also placing the trailer axles and starting to position leaf springs under the rails, though I notice the spring box height conflicts with the rail's vertical extent and will need adjusting.

Adding springs and side skirts...

Writing the window gradient SVG...
